en: A Brief Commentary on the Heart Sūtra of Prajñāpāramitā: A Small Extract on the Prolegomenon.

Question: The Heart Sūtra of Prajñā is recited by every household and expounded by every door; Master Xianshou’s brief commentary has long been preserved within the scriptural repositories for both Chan and lecture traditions.
The two families have long since placed [this text] upon a high pavilion. Why is it that what is now excerpted and abridged is alone upheld as the essential core? The answer is:
Formerly, when Emperor Xuanzong asked the Venerable Dushun to praise the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, he said: "How great is this scripture of the Dharmadhātu!
Were it not for one who has ascended to the stages (*bhūmi*), how could one unravel its text or perceive its Dharma? I shall establish its gateway to demonstrate it. Thereupon—

The *Dharmadhātudarśana* was transmitted from Emperor [Xuanzong] to Yunhua; Yunhua transmitted it to Xianshou. After two further generations, it reached Qingliang and Guishan, each of whom composed commentaries upon it, whereby its transmission first flourished. Xianshou’s compositions were vast and profound; why then did he conceal this gateway of contemplation, sealing it away with locks? He analyzed the subtle and pierced through the membrane, leaving it for later sages to discover. In my private heart, I have harbored doubts regarding this obscurity. [The text continues: ...I humbly beseech you to grant me your compassionate instruction. I am a man of humble talent and shallow learning, yet I have long cherished the aspiration to propagate the Dharma. However, I fear that my efforts may be in vain, like a blind person trying to grasp the moon. I pray that you will not withhold your guidance but instead bestow your great compassion upon me. I shall forever cherish this as a treasure of my life. I have heard that the Tathāgata, out of his great compassion, manifested in this world to turn the wheel of the Dharma and save sentient beings. Yet, because sentient beings’ karmic obstacles are heavy, they fail to perceive the Buddha’s true body. Thus, the Buddha manifests transformation bodies to teach and transform them. These transformation bodies appear according to what is appropriate, sometimes manifesting in the form of a śrāvaka, sometimes as a pratyekabuddha, and sometimes as a bodhisattva. Furthermore, the Buddha’s power of expedient means is inconceivable; he can manifest in various forms to guide those who are lost. This is why the Buddha’s teachings are so diverse and his methods so manifold. However, if one does not understand the fundamental principle, one will be confused by these diverse manifestations.

Therefore, the Buddha taught the *Dharmadhātudarśana* to reveal the single, true nature of all phenomena. This teaching is like a bright lamp in the darkness, capable of illuminating the path for all. If one can enter this gate of contemplation, one will realize that the myriad phenomena are originally empty and quiescent, and that the mind and the dharmas are non-dual. This is the ultimate goal of the Buddha’s teaching. I pray that you will take pity on my ignorance and grant me the opportunity to study this profound doctrine. May I, through your grace, attain liberation and benefit all beings. I prostrate myself before you with utmost sincerity. [End of excerpt]
I pondered this in silence, yet could not find its explanation. Subsequently, I read the *Lüeshu* (Brief Commentary) on the *Heart Sūtra*, searching through it repeatedly for a long time.
Then, I sighed deeply and said: "It was never the case that Master Xianshou failed to explain the *Fajieguan* (Contemplation of the Dharma Realm).

What he called 'opening its pivot and key' and 'knocking at the door to enter' was, in fact, already a distillation of the fundamental and essential points, summarized and entrusted to this brief commentary."
Within this, those in the world who truly know it are rare. How great is the gateway of the Dharma-realm! These three Dharma-gates are like the three eyes of heaven:

towering and majestic, profound and serene; one stands back from them with no ground to stand upon. Those who wish to enter these gates cannot do so without passing through the threshold or turning the key of the pivot.
Yet, by a mere snap of the fingers, the gate opens, and with a single moment of resolve (*kṣaṇa*), one gains entry. One who wishes to open [it]...
The pivot and key to many gates must begin with one gate; to open the pivots and keys of the subsequent gates, one must begin with the first gate.
What is meant by the "one gate"? What is meant by the "first gate"? It is the First Contemplation of True Emptiness (*zhēnkōng guān*).

When the Tathāgata preached the great *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras, he extensively elucidated true emptiness and the true mark (*shíxiàng*). This [contemplation] distills the essence of the texts comprising six hundred fascicles and two million verses.
The mind is bound and returned to these fourteen lines. This *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* is the pivotal key to the gate of the contemplation of true emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*);

it is the first of one gate, and the very first of its initial gates. It is likewise the pivotal key to the contemplation of the three dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*), for all things are summarized herein.
Master Xianshou said: "Only now do I understand how the gate of the dharma-realm is opened."
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, who is one capable of contemplating the dharma-realm, when practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, clearly perceived that the five aggregates are all empty.
This is the brief indication of the text concerning the very dharma of true emptiness that is being contemplated.
The Heart Sūtra is the pivotal key to this single scripture; it is also precisely the pivotal key to the gateway of the contemplation of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Within this contemplation, there are four phrases and ten gates. Of these, the first two phrases comprise eight gates. Regarding the first [gate], "reducing form to emptiness":

the first three [phrases] exclude emotional attachments by stating that "form is not identical to emptiness," because [if it were] identical to emptiness, [the subsequent teaching would be unnecessary]. The final [phrase] reveals the principle.

It then states that "form is itself emptiness. Since all phenomena of form are necessarily not different from true emptiness, this sutra subsumes them under the single principle that "form is itself emptiness.
Furthermore, by stating they are "necessarily not different from true emptiness," it simultaneously subsumes the third proposition:
"form does not obstruct emptiness. Next, to clarify that "emptiness is itself form," the first three [propositions] exclude deluded attachments; they all state that "emptiness is not itself..."
Regarding "form": because emptiness is identical to form, the latter [verse] reveals the principle by stating that "emptiness is identical to form.
This is because whatever is true emptiness necessarily does not differ from form; thus, this sutra subsumes it under the single meaning of "form is identical to emptiness.

Furthermore, by stating that "true emptiness necessarily does not differ from form," it simultaneously subsumes the third phrase, "emptiness does not obstruct form. The following two phrases [are as follows]: three...

Thus, [the first three] manifest both aspects, while the fourth universally sweeps away all traces. From the sūtra’s statement that "there is neither birth nor extinction," up to "neither wisdom nor attainment," this corresponds to the fourth stage where all is extinguished and there is no place of reliance.

Its text is specifically intended for revelation and clarification; as Qingliang said, it sweeps away the characteristics of the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*) to manifest the characteristic of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
This is when Prajñā manifests before one and the contemplation of true emptiness is complete. Xianshou [elaborated] in detail...
Explaining the scriptural text by fusing it with the contemplation of principle, he enables people to know that the scripture is itself the gateway to contemplation;
thus, one may encounter the gateway by means of the scripture, and since contemplation is itself the contemplation within the scripture, one can enter contemplation through that gateway.

Although he does not explicitly comment on the text concerning contemplation, he is truly masterful in his exposition of contemplation. At that time, the *Avataṃsaka* was newly emerging, and his words startled the ears of the multitude. At first...
The mind attains Buddhahood. The entire assembly was skeptical, considering that Nāgārjuna’s attainment in a single lifetime was merely a provisional teaching.
Thereupon, [Kongzang] inherited the legacy from afar and met the needs of the occasion at hand; he distilled the True Doctrine and pointed toward the contemplation of emptiness.

It is said that his commentaries and expositions reached thirty or fifty volumes, yet even a few sheets circulated independently and were held in high esteem by the age—how could this have been in vain? Thus, when he recently lectured...

The Master who guides [us] finds its meaning too vast; those of wild wisdom fear its profound purport. Thus, the subtle texts have fallen into neglect and the wondrous contemplation has sunk into oblivion.
This will cause future practitioners, when gazing toward the gateway of the Dharma-realm, to retreat for their entire lives in their quest to enter it.
I hope that by means of this commentary, they may briefly seek the master key. For these reasons, I have composed this abridgment. ○
Furthermore, there are three gates of contemplation, yet the pivotal key is but one. If the pivotal key of the first gate is not opened, then there is certainly no way to enter the latter two gates.
Sentient beings have drifted and sunk for kalpas, deluded by form and terrified of emptiness;
they fall into the dense forest of the aggregates and are covered by the thick film of ignorant darkness. To suddenly attain the contemplation of true emptiness is, for example, like a fool—
A fly emerges from its hole in the paper; suddenly, one perceives the infinite void. Otherwise, it would remain forever enveloped within the crevice of the window.

When Xianshou commented on this sutra, he maintained that by fully realizing the single contemplation of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one enters this one gate, through which the hundred gates and thousand gates may be opened with a single stride.
Apart from this one gate, there is no other gate. Qingliang said regarding the contemplation of all...
The emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*); this is called the gate of emptiness. The true reality (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena is the city of Nirvana.

This city has three gates. A single person cannot enter through all three gates simultaneously. If one enters through the gate of emptiness, one does not grasp at emptiness, nor does one seize upon signs;
such a person enters directly because their task is already accomplished and they have no need for the other two gates. Now, regarding these three gates of the city of Nirvana:
Through the three gates that illustrate the Dharma-realm, the meaning of entering directly through a single gate becomes clear. The two dharmas of form and emptiness are the source of delusion;
from this arise the ninety-six kinds of heterodox teachers and the sixty-two views of those driven by sharp faculties.

Arising from this, even Bodhisattvas still harbor doubts, while ordinary beings cannot fathom it. Herein, Worthy One, the text eliminates the two attachments of the Two Vehicles and discerns the three doubts of the distracted mind.
Mind and objects merge in profound darkness; essence and characteristics mutually negate one another.

It sweeps away the conceptual attachments of many lifetimes and washes clean the emotional dust of beginningless time. True emptiness is like space; contemplative illumination is like the sun. Thus, all traces are brushed away.
The shadows vanish; it is as clear as holding a torch to illuminate a layered barrier.

This is the very first gate within the *dharmadhātu*, wherein the single path extends vertically to its ultimate limit and the myriad streams are severed horizontally. Lord Pei praised this discourse on the *dharmadhātu*, saying:
"Only after unfolding the maps and scriptures and ascending the high terrace can one fully exhaust the sights of the ancestral temple and the capital. High indeed!
Beneath the terrace there is a gate; only after finding this gate can one ascend. The terrace is high and the gate is deep;
it cannot be opened by anyone who does not skillfully employ the pivot and key. Now, let us use the Dharmadhātu of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra as an analogy for the view from ascending to that height.
The scriptural teachings are likened to a diagram, and the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) are likened to gates. It was Du Shun who opened the secret gates of the three layers;
it was Xianshou who opened the wondrous contemplation of the single gate. Because Du Shun established the gate of the *dharmadhātu*, that gate could not help but be vast;
because Xianshou applied the key of *prajñā*, that gate could not help but be constricted. Regarding this...
To consult a map while ascending a high mountain is the same as being one who skillfully employs a key.

Now, to claim that the ultimate discourse on the Dharma-realm involves the three contemplations proceeding in tandem belongs merely to the doctrine of emptiness; it does not yet penetrate the meaning of the Perfect [Teaching].

This is like consulting a map while ascending a high mountain and, with eyes blurred, gazing to the limit, yet remaining ignorant of the distance to the ancestral temple or the breadth of the streets and markets. Truly.
Relying upon the sūtras to cultivate contemplation, I have first clarified the essential pivot: when one faces the true void with the eyes, realizing its substance is none other than the spirit.

For these reasons, I have composed this commentary. Furthermore, in the latter two gates of contemplation following Du Shun’s *Three Contemplations*, there are passages that exhort beginners and describe how deep reflection leads to clear manifestation.
As for what is meant by "causing contemplation to manifest clearly," it does not refer to a separate object; it is not something...
"Subsequent Wisdom" (*paścāt-jñāna*) precisely clarifies the initial contemplation that manifests this true emptiness beyond all marks.

According to the Patriarch, by means of his own wisdom, he perceives that within the *Avataṃsaka*, the bodies, minds, and lands of all Buddhas and sentient beings are each and every one the essence and function of this Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), infinite and boundless.
Within this realm, he condensed [the teachings] into three layers and recorded them directly upon paper for the benefit of people.
Regarding the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*): it differs from the explanations in the commentaries composed by Xian-shou. This contemplation is as follows:

within the gateway of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*), one achieves *śamatha* by contemplating that emptiness is itself form; one achieves *vipaśyanā* by contemplating that form is itself emptiness.

Furthermore, one achieves wisdom (*jñāna*) by contemplating that form is itself emptiness, and achieves compassion (*karuṇā*) by contemplating that emptiness is itself form. Moreover, through the realization that emptiness is itself form and form is itself emptiness, emptiness and form are equal.

This establishes the three contemplations of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. Furthermore, by relying on the three natures—the imagined, the dependent, and the perfected—one establishes the contemplation of the three absences of nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
That which is contemplated is the object; that which contemplates is wisdom. This is the initial gate of contemplation regarding the emptiness of form and color.

Within the gate of what is to be abandoned, one performs the contemplation of the opening and closing of dharmic characteristics based on the five aggregates, and the contemplation of the reversal of dependent origination based on the twelve links.

The "Contemplation of Following" (*anuloma-vipaśyanā*) involves contemplating the causes and effects of defilement and purity according to the Four Noble Truths, and contemplating the object and wisdom as the observed and the observer according to the two types of knowledge.
That which is abandoned is emotion; that which abandons is wisdom. This is the fourth gate of contemplation, the gate of total cessation.

In Xianshou’s *Huan yuan guan* (Contemplation of Returning to the Source), six contemplations are established as six gates to encompass the mind and lead it back to emptiness, with the "Contemplation of True Emptiness" (*zhenkong guan*) as the first.
One is raised as the primary [gate], while the remaining five serve as its companions. By entering through any single gate, the entire Dharma-realm is fully encompassed.

Now, in this brief commentary, the manifestation of this wondrous gate is likewise so: when the awakened mind is pure and the eye of wisdom is perfectly luminous, one contemplates and illuminates the signless within a single gate;
it is not that one establishes further gates within the gate. The commentary concludes with the "wondrous fourfold true emptiness."

The commentary states: "Illusory form is unimpeded in its arising and ceasing; true emptiness is sovereign in its concealment and manifestation. These merge into a single flavor, perfectly penetrating and without dependence.

The second section of the text’s exhortation concludes by stating that [the practitioner] is sovereign in both the adverse and favorable, being without obstruction or hindrance, and causing them to arise simultaneously and instantaneously.
One should contemplate this deeply so that the visualization appears clearly. The third section is likewise: true emptiness transcends all signs; it is Prajñā."

Manifestation (*pratyakṣa*). These three contemplations are the pivotal keys to a single gateway. If correct contemplation is not clear, one will either gorge on emptiness while intoxicated by existence, or hunt for the initial contemplation while claiming to have attained liberation through many gateways;
or one will indulge in the contemplation of emptiness while loftily pushing the Perfect Stage (*pariniṣpanna-bhūmi*) to the sidelines.

Thus, practice and understanding become contradictory, and the eyes and feet move in opposite directions. Even if one climbs high and stands on tiptoe, one remains nothing more than a person outside the gate.
Thus it is said. Dushun’s *Vortex and Whirlpool Verses* state: "If a person wishes to know the principle of true emptiness, The True Suchness within the mind pervades all that is external.
One does not perceive emptiness apart from illusory form; This very True Suchness contains all things.

By employing a single thought-moment to contemplate a single object, All objects are simultaneously realized. To be able to recognize true emptiness, one enters therein in a single thought-moment, reaching the ultimate."
The net is layered and manifold; wisdom penetrates without obstruction, and thus the task of contemplating the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is complete.

For these reasons, I have composed this commentary (*chao*). Furthermore, O Worthy One (Xianshou), there is a specific reason why this sub-commentary explains only the gate of "True Emptiness" (*zhēn kōng*) while temporarily setting aside the latter two gates.

There is indeed a teaching for this: the Dharma-realm of the *Avataṃsaka* is the ultimate discourse that accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). It consists of the five cycles and nine assemblies...

Within this assembly, which chapter does not speak of the unimpeded interpenetration of principle and phenomena? Which chapter does not speak of the unimpeded interpenetration of phenomena and phenomena?

Master Yunhua established the ten primary gates, which Master Zang expounded upon in successive layers, spreading them out both horizontally and vertically, like clouds rising and water pouring from a vase.
In no place is the Dharma-realm of the two-fold non-obstruction not revealed.

Even in the eight divisions of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the profound principle of the wondrous existence within true emptiness is merely expounded according to the text, scattered like stars across the heavens, resembling the Vaijayanta Palace of Śakra.

Upon the ground of lapis lazuli, they naturally manifest as reflections. For this reason, one probes the wondrous meaning with the hook and sets forth the gateway of emptiness, so that the initial contemplation of true emptiness becomes vividly and singularly luminous; thus, the subsequent gateways of phenomena and principle are brilliantly illuminated in tandem.
Furthermore, this is illustrated by the metaphor of ascending a height: one takes the *Avataṃsaka* Dharmadhātu as the ancestral temple and capital city;
the *Prajñāpāramitā* as the map and manual; Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva as the person who opens the gate;

and the insight that "the five aggregates are all empty" as the method of using the pivot and key. By thus unfolding the map, one enters through the gate via the sūtra; and having bound it together...

Bundled together, one ascends to the heights by means of the sūtras, thereby gaining entry into the gate. As it expands ever further, one breaks open a single mote of dust to reveal a complete scroll of scripture—what could possibly surpass this?
Subsequently, Qingliang and Guishan praised and expounded upon the profound and the essential, using that whole mirror to manifest this half-jewel.
What was abbreviated by Xianshou is precisely what was detailed by Qingliang and Guishan. Qing...

The details of the *Liangguishan* [Treatise] are precisely those that fill out what the *Xianshou* [Treatise] has omitted; yet these omissions do not constitute restriction, and these details do not constitute prolixity.

A thousand nets are interlaced, and the six pearls are threaded through them accordingly. Thus, the various depths and widths of the "repeated gates" of the Dharma-realm established by Du Shun become clearly manifest as keys and pivots.
Those who seek the Dharma through its texts are all companions ascending a high peak after consulting a map. By means of this—
Regarding the Prajñā of Words: when one opens the *Avataṃsaka* Dharma-realm, this text by Xianshou bestows upon one the eye of wisdom.

Guishan initially attained the contemplation-gate of Zhongnan and practiced it for several years; only then did he realize that his deluded calculations throughout many lifetimes had caused him to suffer in vain through sinking and drowning.

Today, through right contemplation, he knows that the fundamental [nature] is identical to the Great Function. During the final years of Qingliang’s life in the western regions, he further expounded the *Xuanjing*; and furthermore—

It is said that one’s mind is not aligned with the Dharma-realm, thus vainly burdening one’s innate spiritual nature. Now, having never yet delved into the matter, I have briefly drafted this to examine its ultimate intent.

Yet, you claim that Master Xianshou did not comment on the *Guanmen* (Gate of Contemplation). Is this not far removed from the "Twofold Mystery" (*Chongxuan*) and the wondrous contemplations? Such was the composition of the ancients.
Each possesses its own profound intent. Do not let coarse or superficial delusions cause you to feel ashamed to inquire. For these reasons, I have composed this abridgment.

Furthermore, regarding the ten gates of the three stages of the Dharma-realm contemplation (*dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā*), the former is shallow and the latter is deep; their sequential order is implicitly contained therein.
This brief commentary explains and clarifies [the meaning], differing slightly from that [previous work]. First, it explains the doubts regarding the Hīnayāna.

Initially, it clarifies that form is not different from emptiness, thereby refuting the doubt that the aggregates (skandhas) are distinct from emptiness. Next, it clarifies that form is itself emptiness, thereby refuting the doubt that emptiness occurs only after form has been extinguished.

The former [point] is that emptiness and form are mutually unimpeded; the latter is that form is subsumed back into emptiness. Thus, the former is more profound than the latter. Next, it explains the Path.
The preceding section addresses the Bodhisattva’s doubts. First, it clarifies that form is not different from emptiness, thereby severing the doubt that emptiness is distinct from form.

Subsequently, it clarifies the mutual identity of emptiness and form, thereby severing the doubt that one must annihilate form to grasp emptiness. The first [of these two] corresponds to the third [point] of the previous [section], while the latter two correspond to the first and second [points] of that same section;

thus, the former is also more profound than the latter. This is likewise the case within the "Correct Manifestation" (zhèngxiǎn) chapter. Regarding the meaning of the mutual contradiction between the beginning and the middle: it is as follows—
It is said that "in emptiness there is no form," because emptiness sublates form. Now, this fourth gate of total cessation is the meaning of mutual contradiction;

for when contradictory aspects mutually sublate one another, they both vanish. Next is the meaning of non-obstruction: the first two gates are mutually identical, as they also act upon and complete one another.
The third [gate] of non-obstruction correctly clarifies the state of non-obstruction. This is followed by the Middle Way of wondrous existence within true emptiness.

Furthermore, eight meanings are opened up concerning the ten gates of the unimpeded nature of phenomena and principle. Because principle is fully present and the text contains [this meaning], there are no fixed boundaries.

To state it briefly: based on the text of a single sutra, one does not depart from the Dharma-realm of the first gate. Therefore, first, by means of "non-difference," one eliminates deluded emotions and reveals true understanding;
subsequently, by means of the "empty characteristic of all dharmas," one cuts off conceptual understanding and merges with principle. Thus, there is both selection and inclusion. There is...

There is both negation and illumination; this is the unimpeded interpenetration of the perfectly integrated and the sequential. Within the text of a single gate, there is the entirety of the Dharma-realm with its many gates.

Therefore, although they are said to be mutually exclusive, it does not hinder them from acting as one and accomplishing one another. Although they are said to be mutually identical, it does not hinder their simultaneous presence and simultaneous dissolution.
Thus, there is both selection and inclusion, and both negation and illumination. This is the sequential that is unimpeded by the perfectly integrated.

Those who expound the scriptures today are no different from this: they invert the sequence of what comes before and after; the characteristics of form (*rūpa*) and the characteristics of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) are muddled and lack order.
Not knowing how to distinguish them, one does not understand where "perfection" (*pariniṣpanna*) could exist.

If one can discern them clearly through detached observation and harmonize them according to the text, then one will know that the meanings of each subsequent stage are already contained within each preceding stage, and that the meanings of each preceding stage necessarily encompass each subsequent stage, interlacing and intersecting like brocade patterns.

[The text] is interwoven; they arise simultaneously. Xianshou said: "Just as a single atom already possesses the aforementioned wondrous existence within ultimate emptiness, one should know that every single atom is likewise so.

This is precisely that meaning. By means of the brief text of this commentary, the gates of the *Huayan* school’s nature-and-character (*xingxiang*), sequential arrangement (*xingbu*), and perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*) are fully contained.
If one merely recites the text while remaining stuck on the literal meaning, one will be unable to achieve penetration. For this reason...
For these reasons, I have composed this abridgment. Furthermore, regarding the classification of teachings (*p'an-chiao*) in this sutra, there are profound differences in depth.

According to the *Qingliang Yuantan* (The Yuan Talks of Qingliang), it reveals the four gates of the Distinct Teaching’s One Vehicle (*biejiao yicheng*). The second gate, which "comprehensively subsumes the ultimate reality," refers to the "True Emptiness Beyond Characteristics" (*zhenkong juexiang*).

Thus, it is clear that this sutra subsumes the Distinct Teaching within the Universal Teaching (*yuanjiao*) by encompassing the Common Teaching (*tongjiao*) within the Distinct. Guishan annotated the *Dharmadhātu*.

Regarding the contemplations: the first contemplation corresponds to the ultimate pinnacle of the signless Mahāyāna of the eightfold *Prajñāpāramitā*. The second contemplation corresponds to the ultimate pinnacle of the Mahāyāna of the same teaching (*tongjiao*). As for the third contemplation being the distinct teaching of the One Vehicle (*biejiao yicheng*), which is utterly different from all other teachings and appears to contradict [the views of] Qingliang—why is this so? Guishan’s judgment is based on two significant principles. First: [The text continues: ...the first principle is that the three contemplations are established according to the capacities of sentient beings; the second is that they are established according to the distinctions between the teachings. Regarding the first principle: the three contemplations are established according to the capacities of sentient beings. That is to say, the capacity of the first contemplation is the capacity of the Lesser Vehicle (*xiǎochéng*). The capacity of the second contemplation is the capacity of the Mahāyāna of the same teaching. The capacity of the third contemplation is the capacity of the distinct teaching of the One Vehicle. This is because the capacities of sentient beings are not uniform. Some have sharp faculties and can immediately enter the profound and subtle Dharma-gate of the One Vehicle. Some have dull faculties and must gradually proceed through the stages of the Lesser Vehicle and the Mahāyāna of the same teaching before finally entering the One Vehicle. Therefore, Guishan established these three contemplations according to the differences in the capacities of sentient beings. Regarding the second principle: the three contemplations are established according to the distinctions between the teachings. That is to say, the first contemplation is established according to the Lesser Vehicle teaching. The second contemplation is established according to the Mahāyāna of the same teaching. The third contemplation is established according to the distinct teaching of the One Vehicle. This is because the teachings of the Buddha are not uniform. There are the Lesser Vehicle teachings, the Mahāyāna of the same teaching, and the distinct teaching of the One Vehicle. Therefore, Guishan established these three contemplations according to the differences between the teachings. It is for these two reasons that Guishan established the three contemplations. Consequently, although the third contemplation appears to contradict the views of Qingliang, it does not actually contradict them. This is because Guishan’s intent was to establish the three contemplations based on the differences in the capacities of sentient beings and the distinctions between the teachings. He did not intend to negate the views of Qingliang. Thus, we should understand that Guishan’s establishment of the three contemplations is a profound and subtle teaching intended to guide sentient beings according to their capacities and to harmonize the various teachings of the Buddha. We should not merely look at the words on the surface and harbor doubts or criticisms. We should instead contemplate the intent behind his words and thereby gain a correct understanding of the Dharma. This is the meaning of Guishan’s establishment of the three contemplations. If one understands this, one will be able to resolve the apparent contradictions between the views of Guishan and Qingliang. This is truly a matter of great significance for the study of the Huayan school. We should take this as a lesson and apply it to our own practice and cultivation. Only then can we truly grasp the profound intent of the patriarchs and transmit the true Dharma-eye treasury. This is the meaning of Guishan’s establishment of the three contemplations. These are the words of a single school; they already differ from one another. Now, I shall briefly set forth my own views. Regarding the first two meanings of "true emptiness" (*zhēnkōng*):
"Emptiness is form"—when form manifests and emptiness is hidden—this contains the gate of "the formation of phenomena based on principle.
"Form is emptiness"—when form is exhausted and emptiness is revealed—this contains the gate of "truth subsuming phenomena. As for their simultaneous existence and simultaneous dissolution...

It does not restrict itself to pointing directly at ultimate truth while excluding phenomena; the same applies to their simultaneous existence and simultaneous cessation. Thus, the universal (tong) never discards the particular (bie). As for why it is universal:

As for why it is particular: it is the initial gateway to true emptiness, being exclusively the principle of emptiness; thus, the principle has not yet pervaded all phenomena.

The small and the great roots of bodhisattvas have both previously traversed the path of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) contemplation; this is certainly not an obstacle to using the Great to lead from the Small.
Furthermore, what prevents the Great from distinguishing itself from the Small? When those of the Small Vehicle hear of emptiness, they immediately fear true emptiness;

therefore, they maintain provisional names to eliminate their afflictions without eliminating emptiness itself, thereby accommodating the inferior capacities of those with small minds. Now, it is precisely at this time that the Great leads the Small.
Furthermore, what prevents us from using the great to select the small? As for the claim that one should not dispel the doubts of the "small" bodhisattvas—why is this?

The *Ratnagotravibhāga* clarifies that there are three kinds of deluded views regarding emptiness among bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*). The first is the view that emptiness means annihilation.

Second, apprehending emptiness as being external to form; third, asserting that emptiness exists as a substantial entity. These three doubts regarding emptiness are precisely what the four lines of the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* refute.

The three phrases of the contemplation of true emptiness (*tathatā-śūnyatā*) exclude these conceptual attachments; they likewise do not go beyond refuting these three doubts regarding emptiness. One must remain free from these three errors.
This is precisely the true emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of the pure *dharmadhātu*. Therefore, the Commentary concludes by stating: "Once the three doubts are exhausted, true emptiness manifests of itself.

The Treatise says: "Because this Bodhisattva did not understand that the *tathāgatagarbha* is the equality of birth-and-death and *nirvāṇa*, being non-dual, they clung to the three kinds of emptiness.
Now that these three kinds of emptiness have been refuted, they have already come to understand the true emptiness of the *tathāgatagarbha*."

It is pure. What further matter remains? The threefold refutation of doubt serves to manifest true emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Once true emptiness is manifested, there is no separate principle to be revealed;

the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) in the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is itself the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). How could the perfected nature exist outside of or apart from the dependent and the pervasive [imagined] natures?

Now, I say that the refutation of doubt merely accords with the capacities of sentient beings, whereas the correct manifestation [of truth] accords with our fundamental school. To harbor many habitual attachments is not the path one should follow.

This is the principle. If you say it was to comply with requests, then why did the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* not comply with Empress Wu’s request, while this scripture alone complies with that of Yingyang?
If you say it was to accord with spiritual capacities, then Du Shun’s *Guanmen* does not directly reveal the true emptiness.

Yet, there have already been three successive layers of refutations and clearings away [of such views]. To what vehicle’s capacity, then, does he conform? This sutra seals the throats of the eight classes of beings and hooks them into the One Vehicle;
the ocean of its teachings is profoundly deep, and the task of its translation was no small matter. Why, then, do you use profound texts to refute and reject, and with a biased mind seek out flaws?
This is the failing of those who follow the Tiantai and Huayan schools, who treat the lineage of Ci'en as something to be weighed and discarded. As for the mantras, they are not translated.

The ancient [tradition] has five meanings. "Strong" (qiang) is not a forced translation; it is simply for the sake of benefiting sentient beings. The syllable *A-ra* signifies knowing all dharmas, while the syllable *Svā-hā* signifies the meaning of sealing accomplishment (*siddhi*).

This is understood by both humans and devas; how could it be limited to Khenpo Tsongkhapa alone? Now, some claim that [the current practice] is merely a biased concession to the tradition of Yingyang.
Only after [the opponent] has become strong may one proceed. Otherwise, one would be treating the secret sections with irreverence and arrogance, and simplifying the *siddhāntas*.

To cite these words and hold them accountable is to incur infinite fault. To oppose such arguments and refute them is no minor flaw. How could I delight in disputation? It is simply that there is no other choice.
For these reasons, I have composed this commentary (*cāo*). Furthermore, the text of the sub-commentary (*shùwén*) is profound and vast, encompassing both doctrine and practice.
It is said: Only by illuminating the ultimate beyond words can one truly know the fundamental source. Yet recent masters, in their commentaries, have been overly diffuse across many scriptures;

they do not seek with precision the principles of true emptiness and wondrous existence, nor the purport of pure and clear contemplative observation. Instead, they extensively cite passages concerning the universal gate, perfect penetration, and manifestations throughout the lands of dust and space.

They point distantly toward the gateway and the terrace, while neglecting the immediate pivot and key. While everything conforms to the literal words, it is not so upon entering contemplation. Even if...

first, regarding the wisdom of hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*), one realizes the emptiness of the five aggregates; the two delusions of views and thoughts constitute "pudgala-śūnyatā" (emptiness of persons), which corresponds to the stage of faith (*adhimukti*).

Second, regarding the wisdom of reflection (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*), one realizes the emptiness of the five aggregates; the delusions regarding the "dust-like" phenomena (*rajas-sama-dharma-kleśa*) constitute "dharma-śūnyatā" (emptiness of phenomena), which corresponds to the stage of the worthy ones (*bhadra*). Finally...

Regarding the cultivation of wisdom: within the five aggregates, both the co-emergent self and phenomena are equally empty. This classification of stages as occurring at the level of the Noble Ones involves four faults.
First, the Ancient Buddha Avalokiteśvara, acting on behalf of the Buddha, entered the Samādhi of the Light of Wisdom and illuminated the emptiness of the five aggregates;
his vows and practices were vast and profound, and his compassion and wisdom were like the ocean. How could an ordinary person of the mundane stage possibly fathom Avalokiteśvara’s insight?

To establish a fixed order of stages and distinguish between the ordinary and the noble is a fault of arrogance. Second, to take the literal text as the ultimate understanding without further discernment:
when that sutra speaks of the "three wisdoms," this one also speaks of the "three wisdoms"; when that sutra speaks of the "three emptinesses," this one also speaks of the "three emptinesses.
This is like tracing the impression of a seal, or copying a mural on a wall, or like a centipede following its tracks and losing its footing. Following...
To grasp the meaning by relying solely on the literal sound is a narrow and inferior error. Third, the true emptiness that transcends all marks is subsumed within the ultimate reality.

While the contemplation of the text allows for deep reflection and clear illumination, I shall now provide a concluding exhortation. As for the *Xuanjing*, its rambling prose creates confusion; I therefore offer this as a solemn warning.

The profound *prajñā* is the gate of the great mass of fire within the *Avataṃsaka* Dharma-realm. It completely incinerates the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) and reduces the hundred negations (*śata-apavāda*) to ashes.
Those with partial knowledge and views, whose "wild wisdom" is but a reflected light, are like common insects that can alight anywhere;

As for the Dharma-realm, it does not transcend this dharma-gate; one merely transmits the lamp and borrows its illumination from within it—how much more so for other matters?

I desire that both the Chan and the Exegetical schools shall hollow out their minds to grasp the definitive meaning, taking this commentary as their pivotal key to seek the gate of wondrous contemplation with precision.

Having read the *Brief Commentary on the Heart Sūtra* by Xianshou, I found its investigation of meaning profound and its explanation of the text concise; though I studied it for years with diligent effort, I could not penetrate it.
One night, while reading Du Shun’s *Dharmadhātu Contemplation*, my mind was suddenly opened upon seeing the text. Closing the book, I felt deep [insight].
I reflected and suddenly awakened to the principle of entering through a single gate into the Dharma-realm of ultimate emptiness. Accordingly, I consulted the sutras and their commentaries;

as the wisdom of contemplation first arose, I felt as though the heavy gates were about to open. However, upon examining Master [Zhi]hui’s *Lianzhu ji*, I regretted that it had not yet dissected the essential pivot of the gateway of contemplation, remaining instead mired within the literal phrasing of the text.
Following the text to record my insights, I have composed this *Xiaochao* (Small Commentary) in two fascicles.

I presented this to Master Hanguang. The Master produced his *Xuanjing Siji* (Private Record of the Mysterious Mirror) to cross-examine it, and as we investigated the various thematic gates (*yimen*), our views accorded perfectly.

"First, among the three contemplations (*sanguan*), the initial contemplation of true emptiness (*zhenshangong*) is the most essential; this is what I [Meng] referred to as 'the One Gate's One,' the first of the first gates. First.
First, the Contemplation of True Emptiness (*zhēnkōng guān*) serves as the pivotal key to the three contemplations of the Dharma-realm (*fǎjiè guān*). Next, it says:

"Second, the latter two contemplation-gates rely entirely upon the initial contemplation to be manifested. This refers to what was mentioned previously: "The contemplation-gates are three, but the pivotal key is one.
If the key of one gate is not turned, there is no way for the latter two gates to be entered. Finally, it says: "Third, reflection..."
In contemplating the initial stage, the essential point consists entirely of discerning through "empty truth" (*śūnyatā*).

This corresponds to what was previously stated regarding "entering contemplation based on the sūtras," which refers to the practice of observing and illuminating the signless (*animitta*) within a single gate. That commentary cites the *Brahmacarya-pāda*:

when a bodhisattva practices the holy life (*brahmacarya*), they should take ten dharmas as their objects of focus (*ālambana*) and observe them with mental attention (*manasikāra*). Among these, what dharma is named...?
It is for the sake of the holy life (*brahmacarya*). From where does the holy life come? What is its essential nature? One observes in this way;
because the holy life cannot be apprehended, one becomes able to accord with such contemplative practice.

All Buddha-dharmas will swiftly manifest before one, and one will achieve the body of wisdom (*jñānakāya*), awakening not through another. Qingliang says: "To apply the mind" means not falling into the state of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
The observer, by means of wisdom (*prajñā*), investigates and seeks; thus, this is the intersection of the clarity that discriminates and examines this true emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

One studies the scriptural authorities: as for the *sūtras*, there are the *Buddhāvataṃsaka-śikhara*, the *Laṅkāvatāra*, and the *Vimalakīrti*; as for the *śāstras*, there are the *Yogācārabhūmi*, the *Madhyamaka*, the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and various texts on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

One interrogates and refutes obstacles and difficulties, repeatedly analyzing and deconstructing them until wisdom reaches its limit and the mind is exhausted; all of these employ the single method of discriminative examination.

the final one says, 'If it is thus with form and emptiness, so it is with all dharmas. How else could this be than through analytical discernment? In the two gates of the subsequent contemplation, it is likewise stated:"
Contemplate this deeply so that the clear vision may manifest. This is not through the latter two gates; for how could it be otherwise than by means of discerning through the gate of true emptiness?

The *Jì* (Record) states: "Because both emptiness and the provisional are the Middle, and form and emptiness have no place of reliance, the sutra takes this as its primary tenet;

"One takes the emptiness of 'form is itself emptiness' as the ultimate truth, and the form of 'emptiness is itself form' as the conventional truth. As for the statement that 'both are extinguished,' it is because form is itself emptiness."
Form ceases; emptiness is itself form, and thus emptiness vanishes. To say that it "exists" refers to form which is identical to emptiness.
Although form ceases, its characteristic remains distinct. Because the characteristic constantly exists while being identical to cessation, it is eternally existent within its cessation.
Emptiness which is identical to form—although emptiness ceases, its nature is not lost. Because the nature constantly exists while being identical to cessation, therefore...
It is extinguished yet ever-present. Furthermore, form is emptiness, yet emptiness remains; likewise, emptiness is form, yet form remains.

Because their mutual identity is simultaneous, presence and extinction are established as equal. Regarding the equality of emptiness and existence: from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), it is empty—this is true emptiness.

From the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it exists—this is provisional existence. Moreover, because they are mutually identical, both are simultaneously absent. Emptiness is not...
Existence is not different from emptiness; existence is not something other than emptiness. Form and emptiness are not distinct; they are as inseparable as water and milk.

Therefore, it is said that they are of one flavor (*ekarasa*). The *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā* states: "When a Bodhisattva perceives emptiness, he does not fail to perceive form; when he perceives form, he does not fail to perceive emptiness.
Because the two truths are mutually integrated, phenomena and principle are without obstruction. Their essence is precisely the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)."
